llm.def: A large language model is an AI trained on massive amounts of text data that understands and generates human-like text. Examples are GPT, Claude, and Gemini. LLMs are the foundation of most AI chat and writing tools.

rag.def: RAG combines a language model with a search across your own documents. Instead of relying only on training data, the system retrieves relevant text passages and generates answers based on them — more accurate and with fewer fabricated facts.

prompt.def: A prompt is the input or instruction you give to an AI. The clearer and more specific your prompt, the better the result. Good prompting is the most important skill when working with AI tools.

token.def: A token is the smallest unit of text that a language model processes — typically a word fragment. AI API prices are charged per token. Rule of thumb: 1,000 tokens correspond to roughly 750 words.

halluzination.def: A hallucination is a fabricated but plausible-sounding statement made by an AI. You should always verify important facts. RAG and citations reduce this risk.

finetuning.def: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using your own example data to a specific task or style. It requires more effort than prompting, but delivers more consistent results for recurring specialized tasks.

embedding.def: An embedding converts text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Similar content is therefore positioned close together — the foundation for semantic search and RAG.

agent.def: An AI agent independently completes multi-step tasks: it plans, uses tools, and reacts to intermediate results. Instead of just answering, it takes action — for example by researching, retrieving data, and executing steps.

multimodal.def: Multimodal AI processes multiple types of input — text, image, audio — in the same model. For example, a tool can describe a photo or evaluate a graphic and text together.

open-source-llm.def: Open-source language models are freely available and can be self-hosted — relevant for data protection and DACH compliance, since data never leaves your own system. Examples: Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek.

vibecoding.def: Vibecoding refers to building software through natural language: you describe what you want, and the AI writes the code. Tools like Lovable, Bolt, or v0 generate entire apps without traditional programming.

tts.def: Text-to-Speech converts written text into naturally sounding speech. Modern TTS voices are hardly distinguishable from real human speech — used for voiceovers, podcasts, and audio content.

dsgvo-ki.def: When using AI in the DACH region, data protection is the biggest hurdle. Important considerations are EU data residency, data processing agreements, and — for US providers — standard contractual clauses. Self-hosted models bypass the transfer problem.

ai-act.def: The EU AI Act is the EU's AI law. Starting August 2, 2026, transparency obligations apply: AI-generated content must be labeled and users must be able to recognize when they are interacting with an AI.

context-window.def: The context window is the amount of text a model can process simultaneously — measured in tokens. Larger windows allow processing of long documents or entire code repositories in one go.
